newsitem.title: USA: K.C. Fed economist upbeat on U.S. housing sector.
newsitem.headline: K.C. Fed economist upbeat on U.S. housing sector.

text.p: The housing sector, a major driver of U.S. economic growth, is likely to perform well in coming years based on demographic and cyclical trends, an economist at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City predicts.

"The outlook for housing activity during the rest of the 1990s appears to be healthy," Andrew Filardo, senior economist at the Kansas City Fed, wrote in the third-quarter edition of the bank's "Economic Review."
"Solid population growth, steady household formation rates, and favorable changes in the age structure of the population all contribute to this outlook," Filardo said.

Many economists have been forecasting sluggish activity in the housing sector due to generational shifts. Demand among the large "baby boom" generation has been a major source of strength for the housing market in recent years.

However, many of the baby boomers have already purchased their first homes and the smaller "baby bust" generation is replacing them in the 25- to 34-year-old age bracket that typically makes up the major pool of first-time home buyers.
Filardo said that demographic shift could dampen housing activity but it would be more than offset by other factors.
Specifically, the Kansas City Fed economist predicted increased housing demand from "youth" buyers under age 25 in the generation just behind the baby bust.
The youth population is expected to grow because of the larger number of children from baby boom parents and because of an increasing number of children of immigrants, he said.
Filardo also said demand for renovations, improvements and tradeups among middle-aged home owners will aid the housing market.
Concerning cyclical factors, Filardo said research suggests that the current stable economic expansion is likely to provide a favorable environment for the housing sector.
He pointed out that stable periods of economic growth boost the income of existing and potential home owners, helping to fuel demand for homes.
Additionally, Filardo said steadier expansions produce lower levels of pent-up demand, making the housing market less vulnerable to big upward and downward swings.
